summary: Provides guidelines for mapping service classes, traffic management features and parameters between Internet Integrated Services and ATM technologies.

eli5.summary: A translation chart between two ways of promising how well your traffic will be carried.

questions: how does guaranteed service map to atm
what is controlled load service over atm

subtitle: How Guaranteed Service and Controlled-Load Service map onto ATM service categories, traffic descriptors and QoS parameters.

tldr.problem: IP Integrated Services describe traffic with token buckets and delay terms, while ATM describes circuits with service categories, cell rates and QoS classes, so an IP reservation cannot be turned into an ATM circuit without a defined translation.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC maps Guaranteed Service to CBR or rtVBR, Controlled Load to nrtVBR or ABR with a minimum cell rate, and Best Effort to UBR or ABR. It gives rules for converting TSpec and RSpec values into ATM rates, tagging excess traffic, and setting Adspec values.
tldr.outcome: Edge devices that follow the mappings can offer end-to-end QoS across ATM subnetworks. It is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 2381 is a Proposed Standard published in August 1998, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It pairs with RFC 2380 and RFC 2382.

sections.title: The Problem and the Recommended Mappings
sections.content:
RFC 2381 deals with providing IP Integrated Services over an ATM subnetwork. It is consistent with RSVP (RFC 2205) but also applies when Guaranteed Service (GS) and Controlled-Load Service (CLS) are supported by other mechanisms. On the ATM side it considers ATM Forum UNI signaling versions 3.0, 3.1 and 4.0. Best Effort (BE) service is covered in parallel and kept consistent with RFC 1755.

The ATM services considered are CBR, rtVBR, nrtVBR, UBR and ABR. The recommended mappings are the ones that follow most naturally from the service definitions:

  • Guaranteed Service maps to CBR or rtVBR.
  • Controlled Load maps to nrtVBR or ABR with a minimum cell rate.
  • Best Effort maps to UBR or ABR.

Detailed mappings are still given for every combination, because the authors cannot predict how widely each ATM service will be available. VC management, such as flow aggregation, and routing are outside the scope.
sections.eli5: There are three kinds of delivery promises: a strict one, a mostly-reliable one, and the normal one. Each has a best matching ATM service, and the RFC also lists the second-best choices.

sections.title: Edge Devices and the Interworking Function
sections.content:
The model has hosts and routers on the IP side and an ATM cloud of switches. The edge devices at the boundary act as both IP routers and ATM interfaces. They process RSVP messages, reserve resources, keep soft state, classify and schedule packets, and police and schedule cells entering the ATM cloud. They also set up, add to and tear down SVCs across the ATM user-to-network interface (UNI). The upstream device is the ingress and the downstream one the egress.

The translation work is done by an InterWorking Function (IWF): service mapping, VC management and address resolution on the control side, and AAL segmentation and reassembly plus buffering on the data side. The mapping runs when an IP-level reservation (a RESV message) triggers the edge device to translate RSVP requirements into ATM VC semantics. VC management can express its result as an IP-level service with some QoS and TSpec, and the mapping then says what the VC parameters would be for a new VC. Whether a new or existing VC is used is left to local policy.
sections.eli5: At the border between the two networks sits a translator. When someone asks for a reserved lane, the translator works out what to ask for on the other side and builds it.

sections.title: Service Categories and Excess Traffic Tagging
sections.content:
An ATM call setup carries the service category (or bearer capability), AAL parameters, B-LLI, addresses, traffic descriptors, QoS class or parameters and extra TM/UNI 4.0 parameters. UNI 3.x has bearer classes BCOB-A (constant rate, timing required) and BCOB-C (variable rate, timing not required), with BCOB-X as a substitute. TM/UNI 4.0 has CBR, rtVBR, nrtVBR, UBR and ABR.

Guaranteed Service needs real-time support, so BCOB-A (or an equivalent BCOB-X) MUST be used under UNI 3.x, and CBR or rtVBR under 4.0. nrtVBR, UBR and ABR give no delay estimates and are poor matches. Controlled Load suits nrtVBR (perhaps the best match), ABR with a positive minimum cell rate (a floor with best effort above it), or CBR as a simple fixed-rate pipe. UBR is not enough, because CLS needs a token-bucket style resource allocation. Best Effort can use any category, but UBR is natural and ABR was designed for TCP/IP-style data.

Each ATM cell has a Cell Loss Priority (CLP) bit. Cells with CLP=1 are tagged and lower priority. Because GS and CLS require excess traffic to be treated as best effort, tagging SHOULD always be chosen if supported. For VBR, conformance definition VBR.3 supports tagging and SHOULD always be used. The IWF knows packet boundaries, so it SHOULD tag all cells of a non-conforming packet uniformly instead of leaving it to the ATM network, which would drop some cells of a packet while carrying others. ATM standards do not say tagged cells must be carried, so operators SHOULD check actual behavior.
sections.eli5: Some ATM services are like a dedicated express lane, some like a lane with a guaranteed minimum speed, and some like the ordinary road. Extra traffic beyond what you paid for gets a lower-priority sticker, so it travels only if there is room.

sections.title: Translating Traffic Descriptors
sections.content:
The ATM traffic descriptor always has a peak cell rate (PCR); VBR services also have a sustainable cell rate (SCR) and maximum burst size (MBS). The IP side gives a TSpec with a peak rate, a token-bucket rate and a bucket depth, and for GS an RSpec rate R.

For GS over rtVBR the canonical mapping is PCR = p_r, SCR = R, MBS = b_r, using the receiver TSpec values. The minimal requirement is that delay in the edge device buffer MUST NOT exceed b/R, and ATM delays MUST be accounted for in the advertised Adspec parameters C and D. If a receiver picks R above its peak rate, PCR cannot be set below R. Other choices are possible: SCR can be as low as the receiver rate r_r at the cost of a larger delay term, and an edge router with no burst buffer can use PCR = SCR = max (R, p_r), which is peak-rate allocation and usually not cost effective.

For CLS over nrtVBR the mapping is PCR = p_r, SCR = r_r, MBS = b_r. For ABR, the TSpec rate sets the minimum cell rate (MCR), and the edge device SHOULD buffer at least b_r bytes. For CBR, the TSpec rate sets a lower bound on PCR. Best Effort has no traffic description; UBR may negotiate PCR just to learn the smallest bottleneck along the path.

All rates and bucket depths MUST be corrected for header and segmentation overhead, since IP uses bytes and ATM uses cells.
sections.eli5: The IP side says how fast and how bursty your traffic is. The RFC gives recipes to convert those numbers into the ATM numbers, with extra waiting room at the border for sudden bursts.

sections.title: QoS Classes, Delay and Adspec Parameters
sections.content:
UNI 3.x signals quality with a single QoS Class, an index into a network-specific table. TM/UNI 4.0 can signal Cell Loss Ratio (CLR), Cell Transfer Delay (CTD) and Cell Delay Variation (CDV) individually. The mapping sets QoS Class 0 for UBR and ABR (as REQUIRED), 1 for CBR and rtVBR, and 3 for nrtVBR. The class follows the ATM category, not the IP service, and MUST NOT be used to add real-time behavior to a non-real-time service.

The ingress router SHOULD keep a table for the egress routers it may open VCs to, with the Minimum Path Latency (MPL) and queueing delay estimate D_ATM. A new VC then gets CDV = D_ATM and CTD = D_ATM + MPL. The ingress router MUST choose a CLR that gives the right IP-level packet loss rate, accounting for packet sizes and Frame Discard mode. For IP over ATM, Frame Discard MUST always be indicated if available.

The GS maximum delay is delay <= b_r/R + C_TOT/R + D_TOT + MPL. The ATM network is represented as a pure delay element: C_ATM is zero and the variable delay goes into D_ATM. The receiver's slack term can relax the requested values, as CTD = D_ATM + MPL + S_ATM and CDV = D_ATM + S_ATM.

For the path characterization parameters in PATH messages, GS and CLS service-specific break bits MUST be set if the service is inadequately supported. The advertised path MTU parameter SHOULD be 9188 bytes, the default MTU for AAL-5. At multipoint VCs, egress routers MUST correct per-branch values such as available path bandwidth and minimum path latency.
sections.eli5: The delivery time you are promised is built by adding up each stop's delay. The ATM section adds its own delay to the total, and the receiver can say how much extra wait it can accept.

sections.title: VC Setup Parameter Tables
sections.content:
Sections 5 to 7 give field-by-field ATM setup tables for each service and category. They assume point-to-multipoint connections with the backward channel unused. AAL type 5 is used with the maximum SDU size set from the receiver TSpec packet size M plus 8 bytes, and LLC/SNAP encapsulation SHOULD be supported as the default.

  • GS: rtVBR with conformance VBR.3 and tagging requested MEETS the requirements. CBR also MEETS them, but has no tagging, so excess traffic MUST go on a separate VC. nrtVBR is NOT RECOMMENDED, and ABR and UBR do NOT meet GS requirements.
  • CLS: nrtVBR MEETS the requirements. ABR meets them when MCR is set to the CLS TSpec rate. CBR meets them if excess traffic uses a separate VC. rtVBR meets them but is not preferred. UBR does NOT meet them.
  • BE: UBR is the best match, with a 9188 byte SDU size, QoS Class 0 and the best effort indicator included. The tables are given for completeness, since the IETF ION documents are definitive for Best Effort.

For UNI 3.0 and 3.1, GS is supported through CBR only, because BCOB-C does not represent real-time behavior, while CLS maps to the nrtVBR-equivalent encoding.
sections.eli5: The last big part is a set of order forms: for each type of promise and each type of ATM lane, which boxes to tick. Some combinations meet the promise, and some do not.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC notes that IP Integrated Services (including RSVP) and ATM are both complex resource reservation systems, so complex feature interactions should be expected. Differing billing styles are a concern, since RESV messages can set up VCs. A user paying a flat rate for non-RSVP-aware service could send a RESV that reaches an ATM network with usage-sensitive billing. Insufficient authentication could then lead to accidental billing of an innocent third party, theft of service, or denial of service through high volumes of reservations.

The different handling of excess traffic could also allow denial of service, with the ATM network spending bandwidth, buffers or switch processor cycles to accommodate excess traffic that the internet service admitted. These problems may be worse where the IP-ATM edge is an administrative boundary between providers. At the time of writing, the ATM Forum Security Working Group was defining ATM-level data encryption and signalling authentication.
sections.eli5: Because asking for a reserved lane can cost money on the other network, someone could ask on your behalf, or flood the system with requests. Good checks of who is asking are needed.
